hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Amazon's original Dynamo was built so the shopping cart is 'always writable'. Which design choice most directly reflects this?
options: Single-leader replication with synchronous followers
Leaderless replication with sloppy quorums, accepting writes during failures and reconciling later
Two-phase commit across all replicas for each write
Rejecting writes whenever any replica is unreachable
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: Dynamo chose availability: any reachable nodes can accept a write (sloppy quorum + hinted handoff), and conflicting versions are reconciled on read. 2PC and strict replica requirements give up availability during failures.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store, a client sends a PUT to any node. What role does that node play?
options: It becomes the permanent leader for that key
It rejects the request unless it owns the key
It acts as coordinator, forwarding the write to the key's N replicas and waiting for W acks
It stores the value locally and gossips it eventually
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: Any node can coordinate: it finds the key's preference list on the ring, sends the write to the N replicas and replies once W acknowledge. There's no per-key leader, and it doesn't rely on gossip to spread data.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Dynamo uses vector clocks. A read returns two versions whose clocks are [A:2, B:1] and [A:1, B:2]. What does this mean?
options: The versions are concurrent; both are returned as siblings for the client to reconcile
[A:2, B:1] is newer because A has a higher counter
[A:1, B:2] is newer because B was written last
The data is corrupt and must be restored from backup
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: Neither clock dominates the other (each is higher in one entry), so the writes were concurrent. Dynamo returns both and the application merges them, e.g. a union of cart items. Comparing a single node's counter is the common mistake.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Cassandra resolves conflicting writes to the same cell with last-write-wins by timestamp. What's the main risk compared with Dynamo's vector clocks?
options: Reads become slower because siblings must be merged
Writes are rejected when timestamps are equal
It requires a central timestamp oracle
Concurrent updates are silently lost, and clock skew can drop the truly later write
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: LWW keeps one value and throws away the rest without telling anyone, and with skewed clocks it can keep the older one. Vector clocks detect concurrency and keep siblings instead, at the cost of pushing merges to the client.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Which storage engine design do Cassandra and many Dynamo-inspired stores use for write-heavy workloads?
options: B-tree pages updated in place
An LSM tree: commit log + in-memory memtable, flushed to immutable SSTables and compacted
A single append-only file scanned on every read
An in-memory hash table with no persistence
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: LSM trees turn random writes into sequential appends (commit log, then memtable flushes) and merge SSTables in the background. Reads may check several SSTables, helped by Bloom filters. B-trees update pages in place, which costs more random I/O on writes.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: In Cassandra, a key is deleted, but a replica that was down during the delete comes back after gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) without repair having run. What can happen?
options: The delete is automatically re-sent to the replica
The cluster refuses to start the replica
The deleted data reappears ('zombie' resurrection) because the tombstones were already purged elsewhere
Nothing; tombstones live forever
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: After gc_grace_seconds, compaction can purge tombstones. A replica that missed the delete still has the old value, and with no tombstone left to override it, repair spreads it back. That's why repair must run more often than gc_grace_seconds.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Designing a distributed key-value store for an interview, you're asked to support values up to 1 MB, about 10 billion keys, and 99.9th percentile reads under 10 ms. Which architecture is most appropriate?
options: Consistent-hashing ring with replication and an LSM-based storage engine on each node
A single large PostgreSQL instance with a key-value table
A shared NFS volume mounted by all application servers
A blockchain ledger for strong auditability
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: Partitioning on a ring with replicas spreads 10B keys and load over many machines, and LSM storage handles heavy writes with fast key reads. One Postgres instance won't hold or serve that scale, and NFS or a blockchain can't meet the latency target.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Which techniques were part of Amazon's original Dynamo design? Select all that apply.
options: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes
Vector clocks for versioning
Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff
Merkle trees for anti-entropy
Raft consensus for every write
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: The 2007 Dynamo paper combines consistent hashing (with vnodes), vector clocks, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy and gossip-based membership. It avoids consensus on the write path, so no Raft.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: Which consequences come with a Dynamo-style AP design? Select all that apply.
options: Clients may read stale data
Applications may need to merge conflicting versions
Background repair is needed to converge replicas
Multi-key ACID transactions are provided by default
The system keeps accepting writes during some network partitions
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: Choosing availability means stale reads, possible conflicts, repair processes, and writes accepted during partitions. Dynamo-style stores don't give multi-key ACID transactions by default; those need coordination.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: In Dynamo, vector clocks can grow large when many different nodes coordinate writes to the same key, so the paper truncates them by dropping the oldest entries past a threshold.
options: True
False
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: True. Each coordinating node adds an entry, so the paper keeps a timestamp per entry and drops the oldest once the clock exceeds a size limit (e.g. 10). That can lose causality information, but the paper reports it wasn't a problem in practice.

hld-kv-store:0.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store, a GET for a key must always be sent to the node that originally handled the PUT for that key.
options: True
False
hld-kv-store:0.explanation: False. Any node can coordinate a GET: it looks up the key's replicas on the ring and queries R of them. There's no fixed owner per write, which is part of what removes single points of failure.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: How does a gossip protocol spread cluster membership information?
options: A central master broadcasts the member list to all nodes
Each node periodically exchanges state with a few randomly chosen peers
Every node sends heartbeats to every other node each second
Clients report node status to a registry
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: In gossip, every node regularly picks random peers and swaps what it knows, so information spreads epidemically in roughly O(log N) rounds. All-to-all heartbeats cost O(N^2) messages, and a central master is a single point of failure.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: Why do gossip protocols scale better than all-to-all heartbeating for large clusters?
options: They use UDP instead of TCP
They need no network at all for healthy nodes
They only detect failures of seed nodes
Each node sends a constant number of messages per round, while information still reaches everyone in about log N rounds
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Per-node cost stays fixed (a few peers per round) instead of growing with cluster size, and epidemic spreading still reaches the whole cluster quickly. The transport protocol isn't the reason.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: Cassandra uses a phi accrual failure detector instead of a fixed 'no heartbeat for 5 seconds = dead' rule. What's the advantage?
options: It outputs a suspicion level based on the observed heartbeat interval distribution, adapting to network conditions
It guarantees no false positives
It detects failures instantly with zero delay
It requires no heartbeats at all
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Phi accrual looks at the history of arrival intervals and outputs a continuous suspicion value, which is compared to a threshold (phi_convict_threshold, default 8). It adapts to jittery networks. No failure detector can be perfect in an asynchronous network.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: SWIM-style failure detection: node A pings B and gets no reply. Before declaring B suspect, what does A do?
options: Immediately removes B from the ring
Restarts B over SSH
Asks k other nodes to ping B indirectly, in case only the A-B path is broken
Waits for B's next gossip message for up to an hour
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Indirect probes through other members separate 'B is down' from 'the link between A and B is flaky', cutting false positives. SWIM then marks B suspect for a while before confirming it dead.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: Why does Dynamo treat a node that's unreachable as temporarily failed rather than removing it from the ring?
options: Removing nodes is impossible with consistent hashing
Most outages are transient, and removing a node triggers expensive data movement
Unreachable nodes still serve reads
The ring can only be changed during startup
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Removing a node reassigns its ranges and streams data around, which is wasteful for a reboot or brief network blip. Dynamo uses hinted handoff for temporary failures and explicit admin commands for permanent membership changes.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: Gossip-based clusters configure a few seed nodes. What are seeds mainly used for?
options: Storing all the data in the cluster
Acting as the leader for writes
Holding the only copy of the schema
Giving new or restarting nodes an initial contact so they join the same gossip cluster
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Seeds are well-known contact points for bootstrapping and help keep the cluster from splitting into separate gossip islands. They aren't leaders and don't hold special data.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: A gossip heartbeat state includes a generation number (set at node startup) plus a heartbeat counter. Why the generation?
options: So peers can tell a restarted node's fresh state from stale state of its previous run
To encrypt gossip messages
To pick which node becomes leader
To count how many keys the node owns
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: After a restart, the heartbeat counter resets. A higher generation tells peers this is a new incarnation, so they accept its lower counter instead of treating it as stale. Gossip has no leader and doesn't count keys.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: Which are properties of gossip-based membership? Select all that apply.
options: Eventually consistent: nodes may briefly disagree on membership
No single point of failure for membership information
Robust to message loss because information is re-sent in later rounds
Every node always has an identical, instantly updated view
Bandwidth per node stays roughly constant as the cluster grows
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Gossip is decentralised, redundant and cheap per node, but views converge over time rather than instantly. Instant identical views would need a consensus system like ZooKeeper or etcd.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: A node in a gossip cluster suffers a 20-second GC pause. Which consequences are plausible? Select all that apply.
options: Peers raise its suspicion level and may mark it down
Coordinators route requests to other replicas, and hints may be stored for it
Its data is permanently deleted from the cluster
When it resumes, gossip spreads that it's back up
The whole cluster stops accepting writes
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: Missed heartbeats raise suspicion, traffic shifts to other replicas with hints stored, and once it resumes gossip marks it up again. Being marked down doesn't delete data, and other replicas keep serving writes.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: In an asynchronous network, a failure detector can't perfectly tell a crashed node from a very slow one, so timeouts always trade detection speed against false positives.
options: True
False
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: True. Without bounded message delays, silence can mean crashed, slow or partitioned. Shorter timeouts catch failures faster but wrongly suspect slow nodes more often, which is why adaptive detectors exist.

hld-kv-store:1.prompt: Gossip protocols require every message to be delivered reliably; a single lost message can leave a node permanently unaware of a membership change.
options: True
False
hld-kv-store:1.explanation: False. Gossip is redundant by design: the same information is re-sent in later rounds through many paths, so occasional message loss only delays convergence.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: Replica C is down when a write for key K arrives. With hinted handoff, what happens?
options: The write fails until C returns
Another node stores the write with a hint saying it belongs to C, and forwards it when C recovers
The write is stored only in the client's local cache
C's data is permanently reassigned to a new node
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: Hinted handoff keeps writes available: a stand-in node holds the data plus a note of its real owner and delivers it when C is back. Ownership isn't permanently reassigned.

options: Rebuilds a crashed node from backup
Rewrites the whole SSTable file on every read
Rejects reads until all replicas agree
During a read, detects replicas with stale versions and updates them with the newest value
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: When a read compares replica responses and finds an outdated one, the coordinator writes the newer value back to it. It only fixes keys that are actually read, which is why background anti-entropy is also needed.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: Two replicas each hold 100 million keys in a range and want to find which keys differ. How does a Merkle tree help?
options: Compare root hashes; if they differ, recurse only into child subtrees whose hashes differ, ending at the differing key ranges
It compresses all keys so both replicas can be sent in full cheaply
It sorts the keys so a binary search finds differences
It encrypts the data so differences are visible
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: A Merkle tree hashes key ranges hierarchically. Matching hashes mean identical subtrees, so replicas only walk and transfer the parts that differ, keeping repair traffic proportional to the differences, not the data size.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: In Cassandra, a node is down for 5 hours, longer than max_hint_window (default 3 hours). After it returns, what's needed to make it consistent?
options: Nothing; hints are kept indefinitely
Restart the whole cluster
Run anti-entropy repair (e.g. nodetool repair), since hints stopped being stored after the window
Increase the replication factor
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: Coordinators stop writing hints for a node once it's been down past the window, so later writes it missed are only fixed by read repair or full repair. Hints aren't kept forever, precisely to bound their storage.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: Why are hinted handoff and read repair alone not enough to guarantee replicas converge?
options: They only work when every replica is up
Hints can be lost or expire, and read repair only fixes keys that are read
They both require strong consistency
They only work with range partitioning
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: A stand-in node can die with its hints, hint windows expire, and rarely read keys never trigger read repair. Merkle-tree anti-entropy repair periodically compares full ranges to catch everything else.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: A Merkle tree covers a replica's whole token range, and the data changes constantly. What's a practical challenge?
options: Merkle trees can't handle more than 1,000 keys
Hash collisions make every comparison fail
Merkle trees only work in single-leader systems
Building trees requires reading and hashing the data, and ranges change when nodes join or leave, forcing rebuilds
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: Building a Merkle tree means scanning and hashing the data (heavy I/O), and changes to token ownership invalidate the trees. Dynamo noted this cost on node changes. Repairs are scheduled and throttled for this reason.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: Key K's home replicas are A, B and C (N = 3, W = 2, sloppy quorum). B and C are down, so the write is acknowledged by A plus stand-in node D, which holds a hint for B. D then dies permanently before handing off. What's the state of the write?
options: It exists only on A until repair copies it to B and C, so losing A now would lose it
It's safely on three replicas because the write was acknowledged
It's recovered automatically because gossip spreads D's hints to other nodes
It was never acknowledged, because W counts only home replicas
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: Sloppy quorum counted D toward W = 2, but D was only a stand-in. With D gone, A holds the sole copy until anti-entropy repair reaches B and C. Hints aren't spread by gossip, so they die with D.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: Which mechanisms help a Dynamo-style store converge replicas after failures? Select all that apply.
options: Hinted handoff for writes missed during short outages
Read repair on keys that are read
Merkle-tree-based anti-entropy repair in the background
Two-phase commit on every write
Vector clocks or timestamps to decide which version wins
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: Hints, read repair and anti-entropy bring data back to replicas, and versioning decides which value is newest or detects conflicts. 2PC is a different (CP) approach that Dynamo-style stores avoid on the write path.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: A Cassandra cluster shows deleted rows reappearing after a node outage. Which practices prevent this? Select all that apply.
options: Run full repair on every node more often than gc_grace_seconds
Don't bring back nodes that were down longer than gc_grace_seconds without wiping and rebuilding them
Lower gc_grace_seconds to 0 on all tables
Disable hinted handoff entirely
Prefer TTLs over explicit deletes where they fit the data model
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: Repair within gc_grace spreads tombstones before they're purged, and long-dead nodes should be rebuilt rather than rejoined. TTL data expires the same on every replica, so fewer explicit deletes means fewer resurrection risks. gc_grace 0 and disabling hints make resurrection more likely.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: If two replicas' Merkle tree root hashes match, the replicas hold identical data for that range (barring hash collisions), so no further comparison is needed.
options: True
False
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: True. The root hash summarises every key in the range, so matching roots mean the ranges match, and repair can skip it entirely. That's what makes Merkle trees cheap for in-sync replicas.

hld-kv-store:2.prompt: Read repair runs on every write so that all replicas stay in sync without any background process.
options: True
False
hld-kv-store:2.explanation: False. Read repair runs during reads, when the coordinator notices replicas disagree. Writes rely on replication, hints and background anti-entropy; keys that are never read need anti-entropy repair.
